title: Debugging incorrect row counts
objective: Diagnose wrong row counts and totals — join fan-out, INNER JOINs that drop rows, WHERE clauses that turn LEFT JOINs into INNER JOINs, duplicate records and orphan keys — and write the corrected query.
context: Finance's revenue number doesn't match the dashboard, the dashboard doesn't match the CRM, and three people have three different 'customer counts'. Each discrepancy is a row-count bug. You are the one who finds them.

exercises.title: Fan-out inflates order counts
exercises.question: This query reports far too many orders per customer: `SELECT o.customer_id, COUNT(*) AS valid_orders, SUM(oi.quantity) AS units FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned') GROUP BY o.customer_id`.
exercises.prompt: Fix it: return customer_id, valid_orders (number of distinct valid orders) and units (sum of quantity on those orders' lines) per customer_id that has valid orders (include the orphan id 99). Valid = order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned').
hints: After joining order_items, each row is a line — COUNT(*) counts lines.
SUM(quantity) is correct at line grain; only the order count needs fixing.
COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS valid_orders
exercises.why: Mixing metrics from two grains in one query is the #1 source of inflated KPIs.

recall.q: After joining orders to order_items, what does COUNT(*) count?

exercises.snowflake: Same fix; or pre-aggregate lines per order in a CTE and COUNT(*) orders afterwards.

exercises.title: INNER JOIN drops customers without orders
exercises.question: The CRM has 20 customers but this report shows only 17: `SELECT c.customer_id, c.name, COUNT(o.order_id) AS orders_placed FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name`.
exercises.prompt: Fix it so all 20 customers appear: customer_id, name, orders_placed (number of orders of any status; 0 for customers without orders).
hints: Which customers are missing? 18, 19, 20 — they have no orders.
Use LEFT JOIN so unmatched customers survive.
COUNT(o.order_id) (not COUNT(*)) gives 0 for them.
exercises.why: Customer lists, product catalogs and calendars must be the LEFT side of the join if 'zero' rows matter.

recall.q: Why COUNT(o.order_id) instead of COUNT(*) after a LEFT JOIN?
recall.a: COUNT(*) counts the NULL-extended row as 1; COUNT(col) skips NULLs and returns 0.

exercises.title: WHERE kills the LEFT JOIN
exercises.question: Product wants 2025 units for EVERY product (zeros included), but this returns only products sold in 2025: `SELECT p.product_id, p.product_name, COALESCE(SUM(oi.quantity),0) AS units_2025 FROM products p LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON oi.product_id = p.product_id LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = oi.order_id WHERE o.order_date >= '2025-01-01' AND o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned') GROUP BY p.product_id, p.product_name`.
exercises.prompt: Fix it: return product_id, product_name and units_2025 (sum of quantity on valid orders — order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned') — dated on or after '2025-01-01'; 0 if none) for all 25 products.
hints: A WHERE condition on the right table is false/NULL for unmatched rows — they get filtered out.
Filter the lines in a CTE (or in the ON clause) BEFORE the LEFT JOIN to products.

WITH lines_2025 AS (SELECT oi.product_id, oi.quantity FROM order_items oi JOIN orders o ... WHERE ...) SELECT p.product_id, p.product_name, COALESCE(SUM(l.quantity),0) AS units_2025 FROM products p LEFT JOIN lines_2025 l ... GROUP BY ...;
exercises.why: A subtle trap: putting the date filter into the second LEFT JOIN's ON clause would keep 2024 lines with NULL orders and still count their quantity. Filtering the lines as a unit avoids both traps.

recall.q: Why does WHERE o.order_date >= ... turn a LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN?
recall.a: For unmatched rows o.order_date is NULL, the comparison is not true, so WHERE removes them.

exercises.snowflake: Same CTE approach; ZEROIFNULL(SUM(l.quantity)) AS units_2025.

exercises.title: Duplicate order lines double-count revenue
exercises.question: Lines 149 and 150 are exact copies (same order, product, quantity, price) of lines 21 and 96 — a loader re-sent them. Finance wants revenue with duplicates removed.
exercises.prompt: Return one row with total_lines (all order_items rows), distinct_lines (rows after removing duplicates — a duplicate has the same order_id, product_id, quantity and unit_price as a line with a lower order_item_id), and gross_revenue_dedup = gross revenue of valid orders computed on de-duplicated lines, rounded to 2 decimals. Valid orders = order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned'); gross revenue = SUM(quantity * unit_price) over those orders' order_items lines (never products.list_price).
hints: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY order_id, product_id, quantity, unit_price ORDER BY order_item_id) numbers the copies.
Keep rn = 1, then compute counts and revenue from the de-duplicated set.

WITH ranked AS (...), dedup AS (SELECT * FROM ranked WHERE rn = 1) SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM order_items) AS total_lines, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM dedup) AS distinct_lines, (SELECT ROUND(SUM(...),2) FROM dedup d JOIN orders o ... WHERE ...) AS gross_revenue_dedup;
exercises.why: Only line 150 affects revenue (149 belongs to cancelled order 9) — exactly the kind of detail you must be able to explain when your number differs from someone else's by 96.90.

recall.q: How do you keep one row per duplicate group in Snowflake?
recall.a: QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY <natural key> ORDER BY <surrogate id>) = 1.

exercises.snowflake: WITH dedup AS (SELECT * FROM order_items QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY order_id, product_id, quantity, unit_price ORDER BY order_item_id) = 1) SELECT ...;

exercises.title: Orphan order 31 breaks the regional tie-out
exercises.question: Revenue by region doesn't add up to total revenue: `SELECT c.region, COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS valid_orders, ROUND(SUM(oi.quantity*oi.unit_price),2) AS gross_revenue FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned') GROUP BY c.region`.
exercises.prompt: Fix it so the regions sum to the full total: return region (customers.region; use 'Unknown' when the region is NULL OR the customer does not exist), valid_orders (distinct orders) and gross_revenue (rounded to 2 decimals). Valid orders = order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned'); gross revenue = SUM(quantity * unit_price) over those orders' order_items lines (never products.list_price).
hints: Order 31's customer_id 99 doesn't exist — the INNER JOIN to customers drops its revenue.
LEFT JOIN customers, and COALESCE the region so NULL-region customers and orphans land in one 'Unknown' bucket.
SELECT COALESCE(c.region,'Unknown') AS region, ... FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ... LEFT JOIN customers c ... GROUP BY 1;
exercises.why: Every breakdown must tie out to the total. Orphans don't disappear from the business — only from your report.

recall.q: Name two reasons a row can land in the 'Unknown' region bucket here.
recall.a: The customer has a NULL region (9, 16), or the customer doesn't exist at all (order 31 → customer 99).

exercises.title: Average order value computed per line
exercises.question: The KPI tile says average order value is about 97, finance says it's much higher. The tile uses: `SELECT AVG(oi.quantity*oi.unit_price) FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')`.
exercises.prompt: Return one row with valid_orders (number of valid orders with lines), gross_revenue and avg_order_value (gross_revenue / valid_orders), money rounded to 2 decimals. Valid orders = order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned'); gross revenue = SUM(quantity * unit_price) over those orders' order_items lines (never products.list_price).
hints: AVG over joined rows averages LINES. You need one value per order first.
CTE: one row per order with its total; then AVG over that CTE.

WITH order_totals AS (SELECT o.order_id, SUM(oi.quantity*oi.unit_price) AS order_value FROM ... GROUP BY o.order_id) SELECT COUNT(*) AS valid_orders, ROUND(SUM(order_value),2) AS gross_revenue, ROUND(AVG(order_value),2) AS avg_order_value FROM order_totals;
exercises.why: Averages are grain-sensitive in a way sums are not: the same rows give a different AVG depending on what one row means.

recall.q: Why is AVG(line value) not the average order value?
recall.a: It averages lines; orders with many lines get more weight and each order's value is split across rows.

exercises.snowflake: Same CTE; or SUM(quantity * unit_price) / COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) in one query.

exercises.title: Net revenue that ignores un-returned lines
exercises.question: This 'net revenue by year' is tiny: `SELECT strftime('%Y', o.order_date) AS order_year, SUM(oi.quantity*oi.unit_price) - SUM(r.refund_amount) AS net_revenue FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id JOIN returns r ON r.order_item_id = oi.order_item_id WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned') GROUP BY 1`.
exercises.prompt: Fix it: return order_year ('YYYY' of order_date), gross_revenue, refunds (sum of refund_amount on those lines, 0 if none) and net_revenue (gross − refunds), money rounded to 2 decimals. Valid orders = order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned'); gross revenue = SUM(quantity * unit_price) over those orders' order_items lines (never products.list_price). Net revenue = gross − refunds.
hints: The INNER JOIN to returns keeps only the 10 returned lines — gross revenue collapses.
LEFT JOIN returns (each line has at most one return, so no fan-out) and COALESCE the refunds.
... JOIN order_items oi ... LEFT JOIN returns r ON r.order_item_id = oi.order_item_id ... ROUND(SUM(oi.quantity*oi.unit_price) - COALESCE(SUM(r.refund_amount),0), 2) AS net_revenue
exercises.why: Optional facts (returns, discounts, shipments) must be LEFT-joined — and you should verify they're at most one per line, or pre-aggregate them, before summing across the join.

recall.q: Why is LEFT JOIN returns safe here without pre-aggregating?
recall.a: Each order_item_id appears at most once in returns, so the join can't multiply lines (verify with GROUP BY ... HAVING COUNT(*) > 1).

exercises.snowflake: Same query with YEAR(o.order_date) AS order_year and ZEROIFNULL(SUM(r.refund_amount)).

worked_example.question: Why does `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')` not give the number of valid orders?
worked_example.sql:
SELECT COUNT(*)                   AS joined_rows,
       COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id)  AS valid_orders,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders
        WHERE order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')) AS valid_orders_direct
FROM orders AS o
JOIN order_items AS oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned');
worked_example.explanation: After the join there is one row per *line*, not per order, so COUNT(*) counts lines. COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) restores the order grain and ties to the direct count from orders.

recipe:
**Recipe: debug a wrong count in 5 moves**

1. **Count at every step.** Run `SELECT COUNT(*)` after each join/filter (CTEs make this easy). The step where the
   count jumps or drops is the bug.
2. **Check the grain.** For each table: what is one row? A join to a "many" side multiplies rows → `SUM` and
   `COUNT(*)` of the "one" side inflate. Fix: pre-aggregate, or `COUNT(DISTINCT key)`.
3. **Check for disappearing rows.** INNER JOIN drops unmatched keys (orphans like order 31, customers without
   orders). `WHERE right.col = ...` after a LEFT JOIN drops the unmatched rows too → move the condition into `ON`.
4. **Check for duplicate source rows.** `GROUP BY <natural key> HAVING COUNT(*) > 1` (order lines 149/150).
5. **Reconcile.** Totals by the fixed query must tie to an independent simple query (e.g. `SUM` straight from the fact table).

```sql
WITH s1 AS (SELECT * FROM orders WHERE order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')),
     s2 AS (SELECT s1.*, c.region FROM s1 LEFT JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = s1.customer_id)
SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM s1) AS after_filter, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM s2) AS after_join;
```
snowflake_notes:
Debugging tools that make this faster in Snowflake:

```sql
-- Grain check: is the key really unique?
SELECT order_item_id, COUNT(*) FROM order_items GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

-- Natural-key duplicates, keeping the full rows for inspection
SELECT * FROM order_items
QUALIFY COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY order_id, product_id, quantity, unit_price) > 1;

-- Count at each step of a pipeline in one go
WITH s1 AS (...), s2 AS (...)
SELECT 's1' AS step, COUNT(*) FROM s1 UNION ALL SELECT 's2', COUNT(*) FROM s2;

-- Compare two versions of a result
SELECT * FROM new_version MINUS SELECT * FROM old_version;   -- MINUS = EXCEPT
```

- **Query Profile** shows rows in/out of every join: a join whose output is far larger than both inputs is fan-out.
- `HASH_AGG(*)` gives a fingerprint of a whole result set — handy to prove two queries return identical rows.
- `COUNT_IF(cond)` and `IS DISTINCT FROM` (NULL-safe comparison) shorten reconciliation queries.
- Because Snowflake doesn't enforce PK/FK constraints, duplicates and orphans are *more* common in raw layers —
  always test the grain before trusting a join.
common_mistakes: COUNT(*) after joining to a many-side table — counts the many side.
INNER JOIN where unmatched rows matter (customers without orders, orphan orders).
Filtering the right table of a LEFT JOIN in WHERE.
'Fixing' fan-out with DISTINCT on the whole row, which also removes legitimate identical lines.
Not reconciling the fixed result to an independent total.
recall: Too many rows after a join usually means…?
The join key isn't unique on one side (fan-out) — or there are duplicate source rows.
An INNER JOIN dropped unmatched rows, or a WHERE on the right side of a LEFT JOIN.
Fastest way to find the faulty step in a pipeline?
COUNT(*) (and a key SUM) after every CTE/join.
